stimulus.title: Natural Science: Bringing Back the Mammoth?
stimulus.text:
For most of history, extinction has meant forever. When the last member of a species died, everything that species was, including its behavior, its role in its ecosystem, and the genetic code that built it, was gone. Advances in genetics have begun to raise a startling possibility: that some lost species, or at least close approximations of them, might be brought back.

The leading approaches do not involve resurrecting an extinct animal in any literal sense. Instead, researchers recover fragments of DNA from preserved remains, compare them with the genomes of the extinct species' closest living relatives, and then edit the relatives' DNA to carry some of the traits that made the lost species distinctive. A project aimed at the woolly mammoth, for example, would produce an elephant engineered to have a mammoth's dense hair, thick fat, and tolerance for cold. The result would not be a mammoth in the full sense, but it might live where mammoths once lived and do some of what they once did.

Supporters argue that such work could do more than satisfy curiosity. Some extinct animals played important roles in their ecosystems. Large grazers, for instance, may once have helped maintain open grasslands in the far north by trampling snow and knocking down trees, and some scientists have suggested that restoring such grazing could help keep frozen soils from thawing. Bringing back a lost species, or a functional substitute for it, might in such cases help restore a damaged landscape.

The techniques developed along the way could also help species that are not yet extinct. Many endangered animals survive in populations so small that they have lost much of their genetic diversity, leaving them vulnerable to disease. The same tools used to edit traits into an elephant's genome might one day be used to restore lost diversity to a struggling population, using DNA preserved in museum specimens. Seen this way, de-extinction research is less a rival to conservation than a new set of instruments for it.

Finally, there is the matter of responsibility. Human activity drove many species to extinction. If we develop the means to undo some of that damage, it is worth asking whether we have an obligation to try.
stimulus.text_b:
The prospect of seeing a mammoth, or something like one, walk across the tundra is undeniably thrilling. But thrill is not the same as wisdom, and the case for de-extinction looks weaker the more closely it is examined.

Consider first what would actually be produced. An elephant edited to carry some mammoth traits is not a mammoth. It would lack the knowledge that real mammoths passed from one generation to the next, such as where to find food in winter and how to avoid predators, because there would be no mammoths left to teach it. It would be raised by elephants or by people, in a world whose climate, plants, and other animals have changed enormously over thousands of years. Whether such an animal could thrive, or would even fill the ecological role its supporters imagine, is far from clear.

Consider next the cost. Conservation budgets are small, and every dollar and every hour of expert attention spent on reviving a lost species is unavailable for protecting a living one. Thousands of species are threatened right now by habitat loss, pollution, and climate change, and many could be saved with measures that are already understood: protecting land, restoring wetlands, regulating hunting. These measures are rarely dramatic, which is perhaps why they struggle to attract attention. Even the most successful revival would produce, at enormous expense, a handful of animals; protecting a single stretch of habitat can shelter thousands.

There is also a subtler danger. If people come to believe that extinction can be reversed, they may take it less seriously. A developer weighing whether to clear a forest, or a government deciding whether to fund a wildlife refuge, might reason that a lost species could always be brought back later. Even if no scientist makes such a promise, the mere idea could weaken the urgency that conservation depends on.

None of this means that genetic research has nothing to offer. Tools for studying and even restoring genetic diversity in endangered populations may prove valuable. But that work can be pursued directly, for the sake of living species, without the spectacle of resurrection.

Advances in genetics have begun to raise a startling possibility: that some lost species, or at least close approximations of them, might be brought back.

The leading approaches do not involve resurrecting an extinct animal in any literal sense. Instead, researchers recover fragments of DNA from preserved remains, compare them with the genomes of the extinct species' closest living relatives, and then edit the relatives' DNA to carry some of the traits that made the lost species distinctive. A project aimed at the woolly mammoth, for example, would produce an elephant engineered to have a mammoth's dense hair, thick fat, and tolerance for cold. The result would not be a mammoth in the full sense, but it might live where mammoths once lived and do some of what they once did.

Supporters argue that such work could do more than satisfy curiosity. Some extinct animals played important roles in their ecosystems. Large grazers, for instance, may once have helped maintain open grasslands in the far north by trampling snow and knocking down trees, and some scientists have suggested that restoring such grazing could help keep frozen soils from thawing. Bringing back a lost species, or a functional substitute for it, might in such cases help restore a damaged landscape.

The techniques developed along the way could also help species that are not yet extinct. Many endangered animals survive in populations so small that they have lost much of their genetic diversity, leaving them vulnerable to disease. The same tools used to edit traits into an elephant's genome might one day be used to restore lost diversity to a struggling population, using DNA preserved in museum specimens. Seen this way, de-extinction research is less a rival to conservation than a new set of instruments for it.

Finally, there is the matter of responsibility. Human activity drove many species to extinction. If we develop the means to undo some of that damage, it is worth asking whether we have an obligation to try.
stimulus.text_b:
The prospect of seeing a mammoth, or something like one, walk across the tundra is undeniably thrilling. But thrill is not the same as wisdom, and the case for de-extinction looks weaker the more closely it is examined.

Consider first what would actually be produced. An elephant edited to carry some mammoth traits is not a mammoth. It would lack the knowledge that real mammoths passed from one generation to the next, such as where to find food in winter and how to avoid predators, because there would be no mammoths left to teach it. It would be raised by elephants or by people, in a world whose climate, plants, and other animals have changed enormously over thousands of years. Whether such an animal could thrive, or would even fill the ecological role its supporters imagine, is far from clear.

Consider next the cost. Conservation budgets are small, and every dollar and every hour of expert attention spent on reviving a lost species is unavailable for protecting a living one. Thousands of species are threatened right now by habitat loss, pollution, and climate change, and many could be saved with measures that are already understood: protecting land, restoring wetlands, regulating hunting. These measures are rarely dramatic, which is perhaps why they struggle to attract attention. Even the most successful revival would produce, at enormous expense, a handful of animals; protecting a single stretch of habitat can shelter thousands.

There is also a subtler danger. If people come to believe that extinction can be reversed, they may take it less seriously. A developer weighing whether to clear a forest, or a government deciding whether to fund a wildlife refuge, might reason that a lost species could always be brought back later. Even if no scientist makes such a promise, the mere idea could weaken the urgency that conservation depends on.

None of this means that genetic research has nothing to offer. Tools for studying and even restoring genetic diversity in endangered populations may prove valuable. But that work can be pursued directly, for the sake of living species, without the spectacle of resurrection.
